Shapley Values and SHAP ![][image1]

Ideally, we would distribute the winnings according to each team member’s contribution. How can we calculate that?  One approach is to consider every possible permutation of the team members. If we knew the winnings the team  would earn with each permutation, we could calculate a team member’s contribution as the average increase in  winnings from adding that team member to a permutation. The estimated contribution calculated in this way is called  the Shapley value. 

To illustrate, imagine the following team: 

![][image2]  
We are interested in Delta’s contribution to the team. We consider all possible sequences of the team members and  calculate Delta’s marginal impact in that sequence.

What do Shapley values have to do with model explanation? If we think of the game as our prediction task, the  winnings for a round of the game as the prediction for an observation of data, and the players as the predictor  variables in our model, we start to see the usefulness of Shapley values. In a model, we have many variables (players)  contributing to some prediction (winnings). Our goal is to distribute the prediction according to each variable’s  contribution and the Shapley value approach is a way of doing this. Unlike in the game example, it is actually easy to  calculate the prediction for different permutations of variables. Note that leaving out a predictor is a complex concept  – to simplify this for explanation purposes, think of it as setting the value of that predictor to the base level or average  value.  

Here is an example in the context of an auto insurance pricing model. We are interested in the contribution of the  prior claims variable to the prediction for a policy that is age 25, has one prior claim, drives 10,000 miles per year, and  drives a sedan. 

![][image3]  
x (25, 1, 10000, f(x) 2000 \= "sedan") \= 

1\. Take subset of remaining predictors (Age, Annual Mileage, Vehicle type) 

Ex: Take Age and Vehicle type 

What does it mean to “not use” a predictor? Remember, to simplify this we are using the average value or  base level. 

*x* \= (25, 1, 10000, “sedan”) and *z* \= (25, 0.75, 15000, “sedan”) 

Average \# Prior Claims across dataset 

Average Annual Mileage across dataset 

2\. Evaluate observation *z* through model to obtain the prediction, *f*(*z*) 

3\. “Add” back Prior Claims: *z’* \= (25, 1, 15000, “sedan”) 

4\. Evaluate *z*’ through model to obtain a new prediction, *f*(*z*’) 

5\. Calculate marginal impact of Prior Claims as *f*(*z*’) – *f*(*z*)  

6\. Repeat for all subsets, *z*, of (Age, Annual Mileage, Vehicle Type) 

7\. Take weighted average of step 5

Using this approach, we can distribute any model prediction among the predictor variables, explaining how each of  the variables contributed to the prediction. Shapley values are fairly distributed and based on a solid and intuitive  theory, which cannot be said of other explanation techniques. A major obstacle for calculating Shapley values is the  computing time. Because we need to consider every possible combination of the predictor variables, there are 2*k* (*k* \=  \# model variables) combinations of the variables to calculate. Because of this, implementations of Shapley values  typically calculate approximations. SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) is such an implementation. In addition to a  much faster implementation to approximate Shapley values, SHAP also connected Shapley values and LIME, along  with several other previous variable importance methods. While SHAP is a local interpretability method, we can  aggregate SHAP values across all observations to glean global insights about a model.
